grade.first_issue: The central claim that \(S=\bigcup_n Q_n\) is finite is false: if \(a_1=2\), then \(a_n=2n\), so every prime occurs in some \(a_n\).
grade.summary: The hitting-set formulation and bounded-gap observation are useful, but the proof relies on a false finiteness assertion. Moreover, the attempted passage from eventual to global periodicity chooses an impossible multiplier and contains invalid index-shifting claims. Establishing the theorem requires a substantially different finiteness argument, such as one involving minimal accepted prime supports.
strengths: Correctly identifies admissible integers through hitting sets of prime supports and derives \(a_{n+1}\le a_n+\operatorname{rad}(a_1)\).
Under a genuinely finite hitting-set universe, the translation-equivariance calculation for the eventual recurrence is essentially sound.

errors.description: The assertion that the union of all prime divisors of the terms is finite is false, as demonstrated by \(a_n=2n\).
The counting argument only produces a companion prime \(q\) whose bound depends on \(n\), and even a uniform bound on such a \(q\) would not preclude arbitrarily large additional primes \(p\).
The required \(K\) cannot exist: eventual periodicity gives \(a_{N+KT}=a_N+KL'=a_N+L>L\), so \(a_{N+KT}\) cannot divide \(L\).
In the backward-induction argument, writing \(i=j+T_{\mathrm{new}}\) with \(j<N-1\) does not justify \(a_i=a_j+L\); the established eventual relation applies only when \(j\ge N\).
